newsitem.title: SINGAPORE: Singapore rulers focus on "Chinese chauvinist".
newsitem.headline: Singapore rulers focus on "Chinese chauvinist".

text.p: Singapore Prime Minister Goh Chok Tong said on Monday he was making a "Chinese chauvinist" opposition candidate the main election issue because extreme views could trigger trouble in a multiracial society.

Speaking at a rally for elections which his People's Action Party (PAP) has already won, Goh said he was determined to keep Tang Liang Hong of the Worker's Party out of parliament because he was "a chauvinist (who) will be a danger to our society".

"Tang represents those extreme forces which once released will be difficult for us to get rid of and I'm determined to keep him out of parliament," he told the lunchtime rally in Singapore's financial hub ahead of the January 2 elections.

"It's now a political contest between what the People's Action Party stands for, which is multi-racial, multi-religious, multi-lingual society, against the Worker's Party with Tang looking at what race you are from, how many Chinese, how many Malays, and how many Indians are there in parliament."

Goh, whose PAP was uncontested in 47 of 83 seats, has been intensifying his attack on Tang over the past few days. He accused Tang of threatening racial and religious harmony in Singapore, which is 77 percent ethnic Chinese but has significant minorities of Malay and Indians.

Tang wrote to Goh demanding an apology for one campaign statement and a promise not to repeat it or face a law suit. Goh promptly challenged Tang to go right ahead, saying the PAP was ready to go to court to back up it allegations.
Aides at the Worker's Party headquarters said on Monday that Tang had turned down the challenge, saying his lawsuit would have to wait until after the elections.
Goh had accused Tang of complaining more than two years ago that there were too many Christians and English-educated ministers and senior bureaucrats.

"Is he going to object against Hindus and Moslems in cabinet as well? It will do harm to Singapore's multiracial society," he told the rally. "Tang's views are dangerous because the fault lines between races will always be there."

Goh said there was social harmony in Singapore because it was prosperous, but added that if the country faced a severe recession, the various races would compete for limited job opprtunities and the "fault lines" would be clearer.
The Straits Times newspaper on Monday quoted Tang as saying he was not sure of the exact words he had used.
"But I have definitely never said anything which concerned anti-Christianity," he said.
Singapore elder statesman Lee Kuan Yew, speaking in Mandarin, also told the crowd they should not think Singapore was immune from bloody race riots.
He later told reporters, "We've got to see this problem in the context of the next 10, 15, 20 years...The danger is not from (Tang) himself, the danger is in the context of a growing China."
Lee said in the next 30 years China was going to be a very powerful country with a very powerful language.

"We are in danger because if we go along with the tide, year by year every five to 10 years as the Chinese tide rises, so also the desire of the Chinese educated to assert their stronger opposition because they share or reflected a strength."

He said if that happened, "we will be destroyed...because one, our internal divisions will divide us and two, there will be external forces out to destroy us because whatever happens no regional, world power will allow a Chinese base in Singapore."
